summary: Specifies the Time Zone Information Format (TZif) for representing and exchanging time zone information independent of any particular service or protocol, and defines two media types. It obsoletes RFC 8536.

eli5.summary: Clocks in different places differ and change with daylight saving. This is a standard file format for recording those rules.

subtitle: The compact binary file format that UNIX systems use to store time zone offsets, daylight saving rules and leap seconds.

tldr.problem: Software needs a shared way to describe a place's UT offsets, daylight saving transitions, zone abbreviations and leap seconds, independent of any one service or protocol.
tldr.mechanism: TZif is a binary file: a 44-octet header, a data block of transition times and local time types, and (from version 2) a 64-bit second copy plus a footer holding a POSIX-style TZ string for future times.
tldr.outcome: It documents the widely deployed format, adds version 4 for leap-second table truncation and expiry, defines two media types, and obsoletes RFC 8536.

today: RFC 9636 is a Proposed Standard published in October 2024. It obsoletes RFC 8536, and no later RFC obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: What TZif Is For
sections.content:
Time zone data typically consists of offsets from universal time (UT), daylight saving transition rules, one or more local time designations (abbreviations), and optional leap-second adjustments. The Time Zone Information Format (TZif) is a binary format used by most UNIX systems to calculate local time. It was introduced in the 1980s and has evolved into multiple upward-compatible versions.

The RFC does not define where the data comes from; one such source is the IANA-hosted time zone database described in RFC 6557. It obsoletes RFC 8536, keeping full compatibility with that interchange format while adding editorial improvements, errata fixes and a new format version.
sections.eli5: Every place has its own clock rules, and computers need to look them up. TZif is the standard notebook format for writing those rules down.

sections.title: File Layout and Versions
sections.content:
A TZif file begins with a fixed 44-octet version 1 header, followed by a version 1 data block that uses four-octet (32-bit) times. Those times only cover 1901-12-13 20:45:52 through 2038-01-19 03:14:07 UT, so the version 1 part exists for backward compatibility with obsolescent readers.

Files of version 2 or higher append a second 44-octet header, a data block with eight-octet (64-bit) times, and a footer. All multi-octet integers MUST be stored big-endian, and signed values in two's complement.

Readers built for version N can usually read version N+1 files, because newer data either follows the older data (so old readers skip it) or is a small extension that old readers tend to tolerate.
sections.eli5: The file is like a book with an old short edition at the front and a newer, longer edition after it. Old readers read only the short part, and new readers skip ahead.

sections.title: The TZif Header
sections.content:
Each header starts with the four-octet magic TZif and a one-octet version, then 15 reserved octets, then six four-octet counts: isutcnt, isstdcnt, leapcnt, timecnt, typecnt and charcnt.

The version octet is NUL for version 1, or the ASCII character 2, 3 or 4. Version 3 allows the TZ string extension in the footer, and version 4 additionally allows leap-second records to be truncated at the start and to carry an expiration time.

typecnt and charcnt MUST NOT be zero. isutcnt and isstdcnt MUST each be zero or equal to typecnt. The version 1 and version 2+ headers share a format, but their counts may differ because the version 1 data can be a subset.
sections.eli5: The header is the cover page. It says this is a TZif file, which edition it is, and how many entries each list in the book has.

sections.title: The Data Block
sections.content:
The data block has seven variable-length elements, in this order: transition times, transition types, local time type records, time zone designations, leap-second records, standard/wall indicators and UT/local indicators. Each length is the item count from the header times the item size, so a reader can calculate the version 1 block's length and skip straight to the version 2+ header.

Transition times are strictly ascending UNIX leap time values and SHOULD be at least -2^59. Each transition has a type index into the local time type records, which are six octets each: a four-octet signed utoff (seconds to add to UT), a one-octet dst flag (0 or 1) and a one-octet index into the NUL-terminated designation strings. A designation of -00 marks local time as unspecified.

Leap-second records pair an occurrence time with a correction, and the table can carry an expiration time in version 4. Time before the first transition uses time type 0.
sections.eli5: The data block is a list of moments when the clock changes, plus a short list of clock styles such as winter time and summer time. Each moment points at the style to use next.

sections.title: The Footer and TZ Strings
sections.content:
The footer, present only in version 2 and higher, is a newline, a TZ string and another newline. The TZ string is a rule for computing local time after the last stored transition. It is either empty or uses the POSIX TZ format, and if non-empty it MUST be consistent with the last transition.

Version 3 files MAY use an extension in which the hours part of a transition time may be signed and range from -167 through 167, instead of POSIX's unsigned 0 through 24. For example, <-03>3<-02>,M3.5.0/-2,M10.5.0/-1 describes daylight saving from 22:00 the day before March's last Sunday to 23:00 the day before October's last Sunday.

The RFC also spells out all-year daylight saving, where DST has a smaller UT offset than standard time and runs from January 1 at 00:00 to December 31 at 24:00 minus the standard/DST difference. Its example is XXX3EDT4,0/0,J365/23.
sections.eli5: After the list of past clock changes runs out, the footer gives a short rule, like every spring jump ahead and every autumn jump back, so the computer can keep going into the future.

sections.title: Writing and Reading Safely
sections.content:
Writers SHOULD NOT generate version 1 files, and other than that SHOULD use the lowest version number the data needs. A version 4 file should be generated only if the leap-second table expires or is truncated at the start; a version 3 file only if the TZ string extension is needed to model transitions accurately.

Time zone designations MUST be three to six ASCII characters from alphanumerics, the hyphen and the plus sign. A reader meeting anything else SHOULD act as if the designation were a signed numeric string derived from the UT offset, such as -10 or +0530. Readers SHOULD ignore the version 1 block in version 2+ files except to skip it, and SHOULD check that the computed lengths fit the file size.

Appendix A lists common bugs in older readers, such as mishandling UT offsets outside the range -12 through +12 hours, or daylight saving offsets smaller than standard time as in Ireland, and workarounds for writers. The RFC also notes that translating abbreviations for other languages is the reader's job.
sections.eli5: There are simple manners for both writers and readers: use the simplest edition that works, keep the zone names short and plain, and double-check the file is as long as it says.

sections.title: Media Types and TZDIST
sections.content:
Section 9 registers two media types: application/tzif for files without leap-second records (where leapcnt MUST be zero) and application/tzif-leap for files that include them as necessary.

A Time Zone Data Distribution Service (TZDIST, RFC 7808) MAY serve TZif. If it does, it MUST list application/tzif in its capabilities response, and it MUST NOT advertise application/tzif-leap without also advertising application/tzif. Clients MUST use the HTTP Accept header field to state which format they want.

A TZDIST service MAY truncate data. When truncating the start, it supplies a first transition at the start point and makes time type 0 a placeholder for unspecified local time. When truncating the end, it supplies a last transition at the end point and an empty TZ string. Clients SHOULD NOT use a truncated file for timestamps outside its range.
sections.eli5: When a server hands out these files, it labels them with a special name so the receiver knows what is inside. If it only has part of the story, it marks the missing parts as unknown rather than guessing.

sections.title: Security and Privacy
sections.content:
TZif contains no executable code and no extensible areas that could hold any. Because it is full of counted arrays, all counts should be checked when processing, to guard against references past the end of the object.

The format provides no confidentiality or integrity protection. Time zone data is normally public, but if integrity matters it must be provided externally. TZif data sent over a public channel MUST be protected with a security layer such as TLS, since tampering could harm calendaring and scheduling, and interception could leak the past, current or future location of a device or user. The privacy section says the format holds only public data and defines no area for private data.
sections.eli5: The file cannot run programs and holds only public facts, but a reader should still check the file's lists are as long as promised, and send it over a protected connection.

fields.name: typecnt
fields.desc: Number of local time type records; not zero.

fields.name: charcnt
fields.desc: Octets of time zone designations; not zero.
